<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, this project is clearly an open‐source PHP library called “Webmozart Assert.” Its purpose is to provide a comprehensive set of assertion methods that help validate method inputs and outputs efficiently. The library is designed to be used as a dependency by other PHP projects for safer code, offering consistent error messages and type-safety guarantees. It also includes extensive testing and static analysis support.

To create a detailed system design diagram (architecture diagram) for this project, consider the following guidelines:

1. Main Components:
   - Core Assertion Library: Represented by the “src” directory, this is where the main classes reside. The key elements include:
     • The Assert class – central for providing all the assertion methods.
     • The InvalidArgumentException class – thrown when an assertion fails.
     • The Mixin class – which might be used to add extra functionality or manage code generation aspects.
   - Command-Line Utilities: The “bin” directory contains scripts (e.g., generate.php and MixinGenerator.php). These work as auxiliary tools (e.g., to generate mixins) and should be shown as separate components that interact with the core library.
   - Tests and Validation:
     • The “tests” directory hosts unit tests and a number of static analysis scripts that verify the behavior of each assertion method.
     • Additionally, configuration files like phpunit.xml and psalm.xml emphasize the testing and static analysis strategy.
   - Quality Tools and DevOps:
     • The “tools” directory comprises configurations and executables for project quality tools (php-cs-fixer, phpunit, psalm, roave-bc-check). They represent external quality enforcement systems that integrate with the development lifecycle.
   - Configuration and Metadata: Files like composer.json, .gitignore, CHANGELOG.md, LICENSE, and README.md should be included in a metadata/configuration block to visually show where project-level settings and dependency configuration reside.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   - The Consumer (client PHP application) uses the Assert library (the “src” components) by installing it via Composer. Draw an arrow from an “External Client” component towards the “Core Assertion Library.”
   - The Core Assertion Library internally uses the InvalidArgumentException to represent error conditions. Indicate this relationship with an arrow.
   - The command-line tools (in “bin”) and testing suite (in “tests”) both interact with the core library to execute assertions or perform code generation. Represent these interactions with directional arrows.
   - The Quality Tools (in “tools”) are deployed externally (or run as a part of the CI/CD, as indicated by .github/workflows) and point to the code (src and tests) to perform static analysis, formatting, and backward compatibility checks.

3. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   - Modularity: The library is clearly designed in a highly modular way (separating assertion logic, exception handling, and mixin generation).
   - Layered Architecture: The core business logic (assertion methods in Assert) is cleanly separated from utility code (command-line scripts, tests, and quality checks).
   - Extensibility: The README details how to extend and override methods in the Assert class. This extensibility should be highlighted as a design principle.

4. Technologies & Frameworks:
   - PHP (as the language of the project).
   - Composer for dependency management.
   - PHPUnit for testing and psalm for static analysis.
   - External tools for coding style and BC checks (php-cs-fixer, roave-bc-check).

5. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines:
   - For an open-source library like this, focus on the core functionality (assertion methods) and how it can be integrated and extended by consumers.
   - Emphasize the supporting infrastructure (tests, static analysis, CI workflows under .github/workflows).
   - Use distinct colors or shapes to differentiate between:
     • Core library components (e.g., src) 
     • Utility tools (bin, tools)
     • Testing and quality support (tests, CI/CD config files)
     • Configuration/metadata items (composer.json, CHANGELOG.md)

6. Diagram Elements to Include:
   - Clear labels for each block such as “Core Assertion Library (src)”, “Command Line Tools (bin)”, “Test Suite (tests)”, “Quality Tools (tools)”, and “Configuration & CI/CD.”
   - Directional arrows indicating:
     • Data flows (e.g., client code calling Assert methods)
     • Dependency relationships (e.g., Assert throwing InvalidArgumentException)
     • Development feedback loops (tests and static analysis reporting back to code)
   - Color coding or distinct shapes for:
     • Library business logic components versus auxiliary job scripts (utilities/testing).
     • Showing external integrations (Composer, third-party tools and CI workflows)

Following these instructions, you (the principal software engineer) should create a detailed diagram that not only captures the structure of the project but also highlights the interactions between the various components. This diagram will serve both as a technical reference for current contributors and as documentation to facilitate easier onboarding for new developers.

By breaking the project down into these clearly defined components and illustrating the flows and dependencies, you ensure that every essential architectural element is captured, making it easier to understand the design decisions behind Webmozart Assert and how it fits into a client PHP ecosystem.
</explanation>
